conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I hear you were just discharged and your upper abdominal pain got worse again. Can you tell me what’s been happening since you got home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It came back fast. It’s like a tight band across the top of my belly and it goes into my left side. It’s worse than last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, fevers, or trouble keeping your tube feeds down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. I’ve been nauseated and I feel really bloated. I’m scared to take anything by mouth. Tube feeds have been going but I feel full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you taking your ulcer medicines—your proton pump inhibitor and sucralfate—like you were told?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I didn’t miss them. That’s why I don’t get why it hurts so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Given your history of Roux-en-Y bypass and prior gastrojejunal ulcer, we take this seriously. We’ll check labs, give IV fluids, treat pain and nausea, and we’ll likely get a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for anything new like a collection or inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need another endoscopy? I just had one recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you recently had an upper endoscopy, we’re not planning to repeat it right away unless something changes. We’ll start with monitoring and imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure always runs low. Is that a problem tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep a close eye on it. Right now you’re awake, talking, and your oxygen looks good. We’ll give fluids and monitor your vitals frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For pain, we can start with IV medication and then transition to oral options as you improve. For nausea we’ll use ondansetron as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin. Please don’t give me those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—no NSAIDs or aspirin. We’ll use other options like acetaminophen and opioid medication if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My G-tube site has a little yellow drainage. Is that infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I looked at it—there’s a small amount of serous yellow drainage but the site looks clean and dry overall. We’ll keep it covered and watch for redness, increasing pain, or pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial bloodwork is reassuring—your white blood cell count is normal, kidney function and electrolytes look okay, and your liver and pancreas-related labs don’t suggest pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so bad if the labs are normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can still be significant even when labs are normal—especially with ulcer-type pain, irritation, or constipation and gas. That’s why the CT scan and how you respond to treatment are important pieces.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so bloated. It’s making the pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bloating can definitely amplify upper abdominal pain. We’ll keep your tube feeds going but adjust the formula while you’re here to something easier to tolerate, and we’ll also address constipation if that’s contributing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night after the IV pain medicine and nausea medication?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The morphine helped, but I still feel swollen and uncomfortable. I haven’t really had a bowel movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That may be a big part of it. We can give bowel medications, and if needed we can use an enema to get things moving. We’ll also keep you walking in the hall as you’re able.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What tube feed are you giving me? It tastes different when it refluxes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the hospital we switched you to Vivonex, which is a formula many people tolerate well when their stomach is sensitive. We’ll keep an eye on bloating and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your nutrition through the feeding tube today. Let us know if the fullness gets worse or if you have new vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about the CT contrast. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function looks good, which is the main safety check. We’ll also make sure you’re well hydrated. The CT helps us rule out things like a fluid collection or deeper infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT abdomen and pelvis is back. The good news: there’s no fluid collection and no intra-abdominal phlegmon. It also shows interval healing of your upper midline incision with scarring and stranding similar to before—nothing new or worrisome there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is leaking or infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no signs of a collection or an abscess on the scan. That supports continuing conservative treatment: ulcer protection meds, symptom control, and addressing the bloating and constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel like my belly is stretched tight. Can we do something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Given you haven’t had a good bowel movement, we can give a Fleet enema tonight. It often helps relieve bloating and pain when stool is backing things up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a huge bowel movement after the enema. The pressure is way better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep bowel meds available as needed so you don’t get backed up again—especially since opioids can worsen constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check-in: how’s your pain now compared with admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still sore in the upper belly, but not that band-like pain. I’m less nauseated too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Since you’re improving, we’d like to transition you off IV morphine to oral pain meds—oral hydromorphone if needed—and acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the oral stuff be enough? I don’t want to be miserable again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it stepwise and reassess. The goal is safe pain control that you can continue at home, while minimizing constipation and side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my regular meds for anxiety and depression while I’m here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we’re continuing your home regimen, including fluoxetine and aripiprazole, and clonazepam as needed for anxiety. If you feel more anxious in the hospital, tell us so we can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried this is just going to keep happening. Is it definitely an ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t say ‘definitely’ from this admission alone, but your symptoms and history fit ulcer-type or irritation-type pain, and the CT didn’t show a surgical complication like an abscess. Since you recently had an endoscopy, we’re focusing on medical therapy—PPI and sucralfate—and symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you tolerating the Vivonex tube feeds today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pretty well. Still some fullness, but I’m not throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your urine output has been adequate and your vitals have stayed stable and you’ve been afebrile, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you look comfortable. Any new nausea, vomiting, or worsening pain overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is manageable. I’m just tired and I want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. If you continue to tolerate tube feeds, walk around, and your pain stays controlled on oral meds, we can plan discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I do at home if the bloating comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your bowel regimen as prescribed—bisacodyl as needed—and keep moving and hydrated. If you get severe pain again, can’t keep down fluids or meds, or you see blood or black stools or vomit, you should call us or come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking sucralfate and the PPI even if I feel better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue sucralfate four times a day and your lansoprazole daily. Those protect the lining and help ulcers heal and prevent flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have ondansetron to take as needed for nausea. If you’re vomiting and can’t keep down fluids or medications, that’s a reason to seek care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, we’ll review the discharge plan: you’re going home, continuing tube feeds, continuing your home medications, and avoiding NSAIDs/aspirin. You can walk as tolerated, rest, and avoid heavy lifting until you follow up with your surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I understand. I’m relieved the CT didn’t show anything scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well this stay—pain improved after treating constipation and switching to oral meds, and you’re tolerating tube feeds. If anything changes—fever, worsening pain, dehydration, blood in vomit or stool—call or come in. We’ll arrange follow-up with the surgery team.
